turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: His misfortunes, you mean? I know them all too well. He has spoken of your treatment of him with such bitterness and resentment that it has left a deep impression on my mind.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware of the narrative Mr. Wickham has constructed. But I must defend myself against such a baseless attack, as it is an injustice to me and a deceit upon others.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am well aware of your defence, but I must believe Mr. Wickham's account, for it is more consistent with what I have seen and felt. Your conduct towards him was inexcusable.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am not surprised by your prejudice, Miss Bennet. Yet I am compelled to remind you that my actions are not to be judged solely by the words of one who would seek to tarnish my reputation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not surprised by your manner of defence, Mr. Darcy. It is consistent with the pride and prejudice that have long guided your actions.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your understanding of my character appears to be founded upon a misapprehension of my actions and intentions. I must express, however, that your accusations do not sit lightly with me, nor do they alter the sentiments I hold for you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your sentiments, Mr. Darcy, are well known to me and have long been a source of pain and confusion. I cannot accept your declaration now, for it is too soon after such disagreements and misunderstandings.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your refusal does not come as a surprise, yet it wounds me deeply. I shall endeavour to rectify the errors in your perception of my character, for they are many and unjust.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your efforts to understand and correct my perception of you are appreciated, but they come too late to change my current feelings. I must adhere to my own judgment and the guidance of my conscience.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: My efforts to earn your respect and trust, Elizabeth, shall continue, though they may seem futile in this moment. I must hope that time and truth will reconcile us.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your sentiments are deeply felt, but they are also deeply troubling to me. I cannot pretend to overlook the painful truths that lie between us.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your words, Elizabeth, cut deep. I shall bear them in mind and strive to amend my ways, though it may take time for your heart to see the truth in my actions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words reveal your sincerity, but they also highlight the gulf that separates us. I must be true to my convictions, even if they cause you pain.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Elizabeth, your honesty wounds but it also clarifies the path forward. I shall endeavour to prove my sincerity in every action henceforth.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your efforts will not go unnoticed, but I must be honest—I see no immediate cause for a change in my sentiments. Time may indeed alter our perspectives, but it must be genuine and earned.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Elizabeth, your candor is both a trial and a beacon. I shall work to earn your regard, knowing that such a task is arduous but not impossible.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words indicate a genuine desire for change, but actions will speak louder than words. I trust in your ability to prove your sincerity, though I cannot promise an easy path to my regard.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your words, Miss Elizabeth, are a challenge I accept with all the fortitude I possess. I shall strive to be a gentleman in every sense of the word, not just in title.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your commitment is noted, but remember that actions are what will truly alter my opinion of you. I shall observe your conduct closely, and should it warrant it, my feelings may indeed change.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Elizabeth, your vigilance is justified. I pledge to earn your esteem through my conduct and character, not merely through words. Let us see where this path leads us.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
